questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a try/except block in Python?
options: It lets code that might fail run inside `try`, and if an exception occurs, `except` catches it so the program keeps running instead of crashing
It permanently prevents any error from ever occurring in the code
It automatically retries a failed network call a fixed number of times
It converts any exception into a return value of 0
It pauses the program until the user presses a key
It only works with ZeroDivisionError, not other exception types
questions.explain: try/except wraps risky code: if the try block raises an exception, the matching except block catches it and the program keeps running instead of crashing, which matters constantly in AI work where a single failed API call shouldn't take down the whole application.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes a retry loop, like the exponential-backoff pattern Chapter 5 builds around a failed call — that's sometimes built using try/except, but try/except itself only catches and handles an exception; it doesn't automatically retry anything on its own.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Python functions and arguments, based on Lesson 5.
options: A parameter with a default value becomes optional when calling the function
Keyword arguments let you pass arguments by name, independent of order
A function with no return statement returns 0 by default
*args collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple
**kwargs collects any number of extra positional arguments into a list
questions.explain: Default values make a parameter optional; keyword arguments are passed by name and are order-independent; *args collects extra positional arguments. A function with no return statement returns None, not 0, and **kwargs collects extra *named* arguments into a dictionary, not extra positional arguments into a list.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Python function that has no `return` statement returns ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 states that a function with no return statement returns None — Python's explicit "no value," distinct from 0, an empty string, or False.

Check the "Add python.exe to PATH" box before installing (Windows)
Confirm the install worked by running python --version and pip --version

questions.prompt: What does this list comprehension evaluate to?
options: ['CLAUDE-OPUS']
['GPT-4O', 'CLAUDE-OPUS']
['gpt-4o', 'claude-opus']
questions.explain: "gpt-4o" has length 6 and fails the len(m) > 8 filter, so it's excluded. "claude-opus" has length 11, passes the filter, and gets uppercased by the comprehension's expression — leaving only ['CLAUDE-OPUS'].

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about dictionaries, based on Lesson 9.
options: `.get()` returns None instead of raising a KeyError when a key is missing
`response["missing_key"]` raises a KeyError if that key doesn't exist
`.items()` loops over a dictionary's keys and values together
A dictionary keeps every duplicate key you assign, rather than only the most recent value
Every AI API's JSON response can be parsed directly into a Python dictionary with json.loads()
questions.explain: `.get()` is the safe lookup that returns None (or a default) instead of crashing; raw `[ ]` raises KeyError on a missing key; `.items()` gives both key and value together; and json.loads() turns JSON text straight into a dict, which is exactly what every AI API response becomes. A dictionary's keys are unique — assigning the same key again overwrites the previous value, it doesn't keep duplicates.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike a list, a ________ can be used as a dictionary key, because it is immutable.
questions.explain: Lesson 10 shows that a tuple's immutability is exactly what lets it serve as a dictionary key — a list, being changeable, raises a TypeError if you try to use it as one.

questions.prompt: Match each data structure to the trait that defines it, per Lesson 10's comparison table.
right: Key-value pairs, looked up by name
Ordered, immutable, can be used as a dict key
questions.explain: Lesson 10's closing comparison lines up exactly this way: list is ordered and changeable with duplicates allowed; dict holds key-value pairs; set keeps only unique, unordered items; tuple is ordered but fixed, which is also what lets it serve as a dict key.

questions.prompt: This prints "demo-key" even though EchoClient's own class body never mentions api_key. Why?
options: EchoClient inherits __init__ from its parent class APIClient unchanged, so the attribute is still set there
Python automatically adds an api_key attribute to every class
api_key is a global variable shared by every object in the program
EchoClient secretly overrides __init__ to set api_key itself
questions.explain: EchoClient doesn't define its own __init__, so it inherits APIClient's version unchanged (Lesson 14's inheritance rule). When EchoClient(api_key="demo-key") runs, APIClient.__init__ is what actually sets self.api_key.

questions.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class APIConfig:
    api_key: str

cfg = APIConfig("sk-123")
cfg2 = APIConfig("sk-123")
print(cfg == cfg2)
questions.prompt: What does this print, and why?
options: True — a dataclass's generated __eq__ compares field values, not object identity
False — == always checks whether two variables point to the exact same object
True, but only because api_key happens to be a short string
It raises a TypeError, since dataclasses don't support ==
questions.explain: Lesson 15 states that @dataclass auto-generates __eq__ that compares field values rather than object identity. cfg and cfg2 are two separate objects with the same api_key value, so cfg == cfg2 is True — a plain class without @dataclass would instead compare identity and return False here.

questions.prompt: Match each AI-SDK design pattern from Lesson 16 to the OOP concept from Lessons 13–15 it's built on.
left: A client object storing api_key and model once in __init__
A typed response object instead of a raw dict
An exception hierarchy that lets you catch broadly or specifically
A read-only configuration object that can't be mutated after creation
right: Inheritance — a base error class with specific errors beneath it
questions.explain: A client object storing state in __init__ is Lesson 13's classes-and-self pattern. A typed response object is Lesson 15's dataclass applied to API responses. An exception hierarchy is Lesson 14's inheritance applied to errors. A read-only config object is Lesson 15's frozen=True dataclass.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about inheritance, based on Lesson 14.
options: A subclass written as `class Child(Parent):` automatically gets the parent's attributes and methods
Redefining a method in the subclass so its version runs instead of the parent's is called overriding
`super().__init__(...)` calls the parent class's own version of __init__
`isinstance(obj, ParentClass)` returns False if obj is an instance of a subclass of ParentClass
`issubclass()` checks whether one class inherits from another
questions.explain: Lesson 14 shows a subclass inheriting the parent's members automatically, overriding as redefining a method, and super() as a way to call the parent's version. isinstance() respects the inheritance chain — a LoggingClient instance passes isinstance(lc, APIClient) because inheritance means "is a kind of," so option D is false.

questions.prompt: Why does running `pip freeze > requirements.txt` matter for reproducibility, per Lesson 19?
options: It captures every package currently installed in the active environment at its exact installed version, so the same environment can be rebuilt elsewhere
It automatically upgrades every installed package to its latest version
It deletes any packages that aren't currently being imported
It installs the listed packages system-wide instead of into the virtual environment
questions.explain: pip freeze lists everything currently installed at the exact version in use and redirects that into requirements.txt, so anyone who runs pip install -r requirements.txt later gets an identical environment — no "works on my machine" drift.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: after manually installing or upgrading packages one at a time, ________ scans everything currently installed and reports any broken dependency relationships.
questions.explain: Lesson 20 introduces pip check as the command that verifies an already-installed environment is internally consistent, naming exactly which package has unmet requirements if something's broken.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the library categories from Lesson 21.
options: Provider SDKs like openai and anthropic wrap a specific AI provider's API in Python objects
requests is the HTTP library this course's Chapter 5 is built around
langchain is classified as a provider SDK, not an orchestration framework
numpy, pandas, and scikit-learn fall under the data & ML libraries category
pytest has nothing to do with AI-related Python work
questions.explain: Lesson 21 groups openai/anthropic as provider SDKs, requests as the HTTP library Chapter 5 is built around, and numpy/pandas/scikit-learn under data & ML libraries. langchain is specifically called out as an orchestration/application framework, not a provider SDK, and pytest is named as just as relevant for testing AI code as any other Python code.

questions.prompt: What does an HTTP status code in the 4xx range generally indicate?
options: A client error — the request itself was the problem, such as bad input or missing authentication
A server error — something went wrong on the server's side
A successful response
A redirect to a different URL
The request is still being processed and hasn't finished yet
The connection was refused before ever reaching the server
questions.explain: Lesson 24 breaks status codes into ranges: 2xx is success, 4xx means the client's own request was the problem (bad input, missing or invalid auth), and 5xx means the problem is on the server's side.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the 5xx range, not 4xx. A 5xx error means the server itself failed and is often worth retrying; a 4xx error means the request you sent was the issue, and retrying the identical request won't fix it.

questions.prompt: In a try/except block catching requests.exceptions.Timeout, ConnectionError, HTTPError, and RequestException together, why must the except clause for RequestException come last?
options: RequestException is the shared base class every other requests exception inherits from, so catching it earlier would swallow the more specific exceptions before they get a chance to run
Python requires except clauses to be written in alphabetical order
RequestException can only be raised after the other three exceptions have already been handled
RequestException has nothing to do with Timeout, ConnectionError, or HTTPError
questions.explain: Lesson 24 ties this directly back to Lesson 16's inheritance-ordering rule: RequestException is the base class every other requests exception inherits from, so an earlier, broader except for it would catch everything first and the more specific except blocks below it would never run.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: most AI APIs authenticate requests via an HTTP header formatted as `Authorization: ________ <key>`.
questions.explain: Lesson 25 covers the Bearer token pattern: the Authorization header's value starts with the word Bearer, a space, then the key itself — the standard way nearly every AI API expects credentials to be sent.

questions.prompt: Put these pieces of a production-ready AI API call in the order Lesson 26 says they combine.
items: Build the request with query/body parameters and headers
Set a timeout so a slow server can't hang the program forever
Call raise_for_status() to turn a bad non-429 status into an exception
Run a backoff loop specifically for 429 rate-limit responses
questions.explain: Lesson 26's closing recap combines parameters and headers (Lesson 23), a timeout (also Lesson 23), raise_for_status() for ordinary error statuses (Lesson 24), and finally a retry/backoff loop specifically for 429s — that combination is what a reliable client looks like.

questions.code:
async def fetch_response(prompt):
    print(f"sending: {prompt}")
    return f"response to: {prompt}"

result = fetch_response("hello")
print(result)
questions.prompt: This prints `<coroutine object fetch_response at 0x...>` instead of the response text, and "sending: hello" never prints either. Why?
options: Calling an async def function returns a coroutine object without running its body; the body only runs once that coroutine is awaited
The function raised an exception that was silently swallowed
An async def function can only be called once per program run
Coroutine objects are just Python's way of reporting a TypeError
questions.explain: Lesson 28 calls this out as the most common beginner mistake: calling an async def function doesn't run its body — it returns a paused coroutine object. Only awaiting that coroutine (inside another async def, via asyncio.run()) actually runs the body and prints "sending: hello".

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about asyncio.gather(), based on Lesson 30.
options: It runs multiple coroutines concurrently and returns their results in the same order they were passed in
By default, if one coroutine raises an exception, gather() cancels the rest of the batch
Passing return_exceptions=True lets the batch finish even if some calls fail, with exceptions in place of results
requests.get() is safe to call inside an async def function without blocking the event loop
gather() can only run exactly two coroutines at a time
questions.explain: gather() preserves input order in its results, cancels the rest of the batch by default when one call fails, and return_exceptions=True changes that so failures come back as exception objects instead. requests is explicitly called out as unsafe inside async code because it blocks the event loop — an async-aware client like httpx.AsyncClient is needed instead. gather() also accepts any number of coroutines, not just two.

questions.prompt: Put these async concepts in the order Chapter 6 introduces them.
items: Why AI API calls are I/O-bound, so a synchronous program can't overlap its waiting time
async def and await — coroutine functions, and what actually runs one
asyncio.run() and asyncio.create_task() — the event loop, and starting coroutines concurrently
asyncio.gather() — running several real AI API calls concurrently and collecting their results
questions.explain: Chapter 6 builds in this order: Lesson 27 motivates async with I/O-bound waiting, Lesson 28 covers async/await syntax, Lesson 29 covers asyncio.run() and create_task(), and Lesson 30 uses asyncio.gather() to actually run multiple AI calls concurrently.

questions.prompt: A debugging session shows a variable printing as `<coroutine object call_api at 0x...>` instead of the expected response text. Per Lesson 34, what almost always causes this?
options: A missing `await` before the call to that coroutine function
The API key being used is invalid
The function raised a KeyError that was caught silently
The code is running inside the wrong virtual environment
questions.explain: Lesson 34 names this directly: the single most common async bug is forgetting await, which doesn't raise an error — it just silently hands back a coroutine object instead of the awaited result. Seeing a coroutine object print out is the signal to check for a missing await first.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: pytest automatically discovers files named ________ and runs every function inside them whose name starts with test_.
questions.explain: Lesson 31 states that pytest auto-discovers any file matching the test_*.py naming pattern and runs every test_* function inside it, with no test-runner boilerplate required.

questions.prompt: Match each tool from Chapter 7 to the job it does.
right: Runs automated tests and reports pass/fail based on assert statements
Reads type hints to check your codebase for mismatches, without running the code
Automatically rewrites code's whitespace, quotes, and line breaks to one consistent style
Flags real problems like unused imports and undefined names, without rewriting your code
questions.explain: pytest runs tests built on assert; mypy reads type hints to catch mismatches without executing the code; black is the opinionated auto-formatter; ruff is the fast linter that reports problems like unused imports or undefined names without rewriting anything.

questions.prompt: Put these debugging steps in the order Lesson 34 recommends for approaching a failure.
items: Read the traceback's last line first — that's the actual error
Read the call-stack lines above it to see where the failure happened
Add a breakpoint() or a targeted print() to inspect the real value of a suspicious variable
If a variable prints as a coroutine object, check for a missing await first
questions.explain: Lesson 34 teaches reading a traceback bottom-up (the error, then the call stack above it), then using breakpoint() or a deliberate print() to inspect real values, and specifically checking for a missing await if a coroutine object shows up where a value was expected.

The CLI entry point plus the API client class
